statement: Kira draws a chain of right triangles. Triangle $1$ has legs of length $1$ and $1$. For each $n \ge 2$, triangle $n$ has one leg equal to the hypotenuse of triangle $n - 1$ and its other leg of length $n$. For example, triangle $2$ has legs $\sqrt{2}$ and $2$. What is the smallest $n$ for which the hypotenuse of triangle $n$ is longer than $20$?

choices.misconception: I compared the square of the hypotenuse with $20$ instead of with $20^2 = 400$, and triangle $4$ is the first with a square above $20$.
I thought each hypotenuse is the previous hypotenuse plus the new leg, so starting from about $1.4$ I added $2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ and passed $20$ at triangle $6$.
I thought the square of the hypotenuse of triangle $n$ is just $n^2 + 1$, using only the newest leg, so I needed $n^2 + 1 > 400$.
I added $n$ instead of $n^2$ to the square of the hypotenuse each time, so I needed $1 + (1 + 2 + \cdots + n) > 400$.

hints: Work with the squares of the hypotenuses instead of the hypotenuses themselves.

By the Pythagorean theorem, the square of the hypotenuse of triangle $n$ is the square of the hypotenuse of triangle $n - 1$ plus $n^2$. So the squares go $2$, then $2 + 4 = 6$, then $6 + 9 = 15$, and so on.
The square of the hypotenuse of triangle $n$ is $1 + 1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + n^2$. You need this to be more than $20^2 = 400$.
